evidence.claim: The assumption of N_max=100 for turbulent torque correlation timescale may significantly overestimate dephasing in MRI-dominated AGN disk regions, as MRI simulations indicate much shorter correlation timescales.
evidence.excerpt: If an MRI-dominated disk implies an N_max closer to 10 rather than 100, the turbulent dephasing would decrease by a factor of roughly 3. The authors should explicitly discuss the expected correlation timescale for MRI in the text and comment on how a significantly lower N_max would shrink the parameter space for detectability shown in Figure 2.

judge_panel.reason: The paper sets Nmax=100 based on Wu et al. (2024) HD simulations without quantitatively discussing MRI correlation timescales or how a different Nmax would affect results. The paper only notes 'Even though MRI is presumably the main driver of turbulence in the inner highly ionized part of the AGN disk...our description of the turbulent torque is based on Wu et al. (2024), which was inspired by turbulence due to GI in protoplanetary disks' as a caveat, but does not quantify the effect of varying Nmax or discuss expected MRI correlation timescales specifically.

The paper does discuss the fluctuation timescale parameter and its MRI caveat: it sets "Nmax = 100, which is chosen based upon how often the torque changes magnitude or sign in Wu et al. (2024)," and notes that "the detailed properties of MRI in 3D are very complex, showing pattern changes on timescales even longer than the orbital time." This does not support the reviewer's specific assertion that MRI implies a much shorter correlation time than assumed.

evidence.claim: The definition and presentation of the detectability metric (Lambda > 1) may be misinterpreted, since it describes a scenario where only ~2.5% of EMRIs exceed the detection threshold, not the majority.
evidence.excerpt: Because the dephasing distribution is assumed to be Gaussian, taking the 2\sigma tail implies that only ~2.5% of the EMRIs in these specific parameter regimes will actually exhibit a detectable dephasing.

judge_panel.reason: The paper explicitly acknowledges this probabilistic interpretation: the definition uses the 2-sigma tail (Lambda = |Δψlin| + 2σ_turb)/(8/SNR0) > 1) and the text in Section 4 states 'the linear dephasing is unobservable (i.e. Λ<1) while the turbulent dephasing could be observable due to Λ>1', with 'could' indicating this is a tail probability scenario, not a majority claim. The paper is not claiming the majority of EMRIs are detectable.

The paper explicitly defines Λ as a tail-based criterion, not a statement about the majority of systems: Fig. 2 says it is used "to signify where the tail of the turbulent dephasing distribution (set to |∆ψlin| + 2σ̂turb) becomes observable," and the text says the turbulent dephasing "could be observable" when Λ > 1. So the alleged misinterpretation is not present in the paper's wording.

evidence.claim: Possible amplification or suppression of turbulent torque variance near the ISCO due to ignored relativistic effects is not addressed and could substantially affect the results.
evidence.excerpt: Because the EMRI spends a large number of GW cycles in this highly relativistic regime, and because relativistic effects generally alter both the orbital velocity and the resonances that drive disk torques, it would be beneficial to add a brief speculative sentence or two about whether relativistic corrections are generally expected to amplify or suppress the turbulent variance \sigma_{T_turb}.

judge_panel.reason: The paper acknowledges not considering relativistic corrections ('We also do not consider the relativistic corrections to the Lindblad torque (Duque et al. 2025b)') but does not provide any discussion of whether relativistic effects near the ISCO would amplify or suppress the turbulent variance σ_{T_turb}, leaving this specific concern unaddressed beyond a brief mention of linear torque corrections.

The paper acknowledges omitted relativistic effects only for the linear torque—"We also do not consider the relativistic corrections to the Lindblad torque..., which, in principle, can increase the linear torque"—not explicitly for the turbulent variance σ_Tturb near ISCO. However, Appendix A also states that "most of the dephasing is coming from the initial evolution," suggesting late/ISCO effects may be subdominant, so the seriousness of the omission is unclear from the paper alone.
